1.title: TI Help
1.overview: Integrated technical support system (mobile, web, and desktop) built as a capstone project, replacing decentralized WhatsApp/email support with a single flow for opening and tracking tickets, with AI-assisted triage.
1.challenge: IT support was scattered across channels with no traceability or status visibility — users resent the same request through different channels when they got no response, and technicians received tickets with no standardized context.
1.process: In-person discovery with 11 sponsor users (7 Systems Analysis students, 2 from another cohort, 2 from Psychology). In the first version of the flow, users picked their own ticket priority (low/medium/high) — in discussion with professors and the 4-person team, we spotted a structural bias before even testing: users would tend to always mark 'high priority' to get served faster, invalidating triage. We fixed it by removing self-assigned priority, replacing it with problem type selection (hardware/software/network) + free description, leaving priority to triage (AI + technician). This was the only one of the 4 deliverables run with a formal backlog over the 6-month project.

designSprint.description: Pain-point gathering with professors and the 4-person team, mapping failures in the WhatsApp/email support flow before any wireframe existed.
Consolidated 11 interviews into problem definitions and identified the priority self-assignment bias before the first prototype.
Information architecture, triage flows, and high-fidelity prototypes in Figma across all three platforms (mobile, web, desktop).
Moderated in-person test with the 11 sponsor users and faculty panel, measuring task time before and after the menu repositioning.
Final delivery as a capstone project scoring 8.5/10, including a real mobile implementation in React Native.

1.myRole: UX/UI Designer and mobile front-end developer on a 4-person team, responsible for user research, information architecture, flows, high-fidelity prototypes, and the mobile implementation in React Native.

certainties: Users didn't know the status of an already-open ticket, causing repeated resubmission across channels
Letting users self-assign priority would create systematic bias toward 'high priority'
Technicians needed clear categorization (hardware/software/network) for fast triage
suppositions: AI-assisted categorization would reduce manual triage time
Repositioning notifications and the menu would reduce task execution time in the app
doubts: Would the triage AI stay accurate at real volume, outside the controlled test environment?
Would non-technical users (e.g. Psychology students) adapt to the flow as well as Systems Analysis students in the long run?

1.userFlow: User identifies the problem → selects type (hardware/software/network) and describes it → ticket gets categorized and prioritized by triage → user tracks status in real time. Technician flow (Web/Desktop): if there's no time to open the ticket immediately, it automatically enters as low-priority/waiting, configurable manually or with a later AI suggestion. Admin panel: employee creation, deletion, and updates restricted to admin, including deleting data of former employees — the biggest governance win the team identified.

personas.name: Systems Analysis participant
personas.pain: Opened tickets via WhatsApp and email without knowing if anyone was handling the issue, resending the same message across channels.
personas.goal: Open and track a ticket on any device, with visible status, without having to chase anyone.

personas.name: Psychology participant
personas.pain: Struggled to describe technical problems using specific vocabulary, which delayed service.
personas.goal: Report a problem in plain language, without needing to know IT terminology.

userStories.story: As a technical system user, I want to track my ticket's status in real time so that I don't have to resend the same request across different channels.
As a non-technical user, I want to describe my problem in my own words so that I don't need IT terminology to get help.

problemDefinitions.definition: Is a technical system user who needs real-time status visibility because it removes the need to manually chase support across multiple channels.
Is an IT-unfamiliar user who needs a plain-language ticket flow because technical jargon discourages them from asking for help early.

craftNotes.conventions: Followed navigation patterns users already internalize (bottom tab bar, bell icon for notifications, numeric badge for pending items) to reduce the learning curve for a mixed audience of technical and non-technical users.
craftNotes.affordances: Ticket-opening buttons use elevation and accent color to signal clickability; ticket status is communicated through color + icon + text simultaneously, never color alone, avoiding ambiguity for users who don't map color to state instantly.
craftNotes.equity: The flow was designed with non-technical users (Psychology students) in mind from the first version — removing self-assigned priority came directly from not wanting to penalize people who don't know how to 'game' the support system.
craftNotes.testing: Moderated in-person testing with a task script and direct observation, comparing execution time before/after the AI change instead of relying only on subjective user opinion.

1.solution: Removed user self-assigned priority → replaced with problem type selection + free description. Repositioned notifications and menu in the mobile version. Technician flow with an automatic waiting/low-priority state for tickets without immediate attention. Employee management and data deletion restricted to admin.
1.finalProject: BEFORE vs. AFTER METRIC (in-person test, 11 participants + faculty panel): time to complete the app's main tasks dropped from just over 5 minutes to 3 minutes 30 seconds — a ~30% reduction — after repositioning the menu/notifications. SUCCESS RATE: 100% maintained in both versions (before and after) — meaning the gain was in EFFICIENCY, not COMPLETION; nobody failed to complete the task before the change, it just took longer. ERROR IDENTIFIED AND FIXED: priority self-assignment bias, resolved during Reflect before formal testing even happened. ACADEMIC EVALUATION: 8.5/10 from the capstone panel. STATED LIMITATION: timing was measured informally, without per-session instrumented stopwatch tracking — directional data reported by the team and panel, not an instrumented usability test with per-task timing.

research.method: In-person interviews, task observation, and support-flow review

interviews.participantProfile: 7 Systems Analysis students, 2 from another cohort, 2 Psychology students

2.title: KaloBurn
2.overview: Kalo Burn is a conceptual mobile fitness experience focused on transforming difficult-to-interpret fitness metrics into simple decisions about training, energy expenditure and progress.
2.challenge: Users receive a lot of information, but often do not understand what is important or what action they should take. The product needed to make training, energy use and progress legible without turning itself into a diet prescription tool.
2.process: The work was organized around three core questions: 'Como estou?', 'O que faço?' and 'Estou evoluindo?'. It combined UX research, competitive audit and design synthesis to define a clearer hierarchy before proposing decision-oriented content and recommendations.

designSprint.description: Mapped the problem of unclear fitness interpretation and the gap between data and decision-making.
Defined the three core questions that shaped the product: how the user feels, what action to take next and whether progress is improving.
Translated the insights into a mobile experience with clear hierarchy, recommendations and progress context.
Reviewed how recommendations could be placed closer to the metric that explained them, improving clarity.
Refined the system to connect score, explanation and next action within the same section.

certainties: Users are confronted with many metrics but rarely understand what matters most
Training decisions become clearer when explanation and next action are shown together
Fitness products should support interpretation, not prescribe diets
suppositions: A simplified dashboard would reduce cognitive effort during training decisions
Contextual recommendations would help users understand their current state more quickly
Progress over time should be visualized without requiring heavy graph interpretation
doubts: This is a conceptual product, so real-world validation with actual users would still be required
The best balance between guidance and autonomy would need to be tested with real behavior data

2.userFlow: Discover → Define the goal → Register → Provide training/context → Understand → Visualize current state → Adjust → Identify next step → Return → Track evolution.

personas.name: Fitness beginner
personas.pain: Receives too much numerical information but does not understand which indicator matters or what to do next.
personas.goal: Know their current state, understand the reason behind the recommendation, and make a clear next decision.

userStories.story: As a mobile fitness user, I want to understand my current state in a simple way so that I can decide what to do next without interpreting complex metrics.

problemDefinitions.definition: Needs a clearer hierarchy of training information because the product currently overloads the user with data without clarifying what matters and what action should follow.

craftNotes.conventions: The experience keeps a compact, high-contrast, low-noise structure to make the user scan quickly and act with confidence.
craftNotes.affordances: Score, explanation and CTA live in the same block so the user sees the metric, its meaning and the next step together.
craftNotes.equity: The experience avoids diet prescriptions and keeps the focus on training decisions, energy expenditure and progress interpretation.
craftNotes.testing: The key validation insight was that users understood a recommendation better when it appeared immediately after the metric that justified it.

2.solution: The concept organizes training and energy-expenditure information into a more direct experience, helping the user understand their current state and identify the next step. It includes a dashboard for 'Como estou?', a recommendations area for 'O que faço?' and a progression view for 'Estou evoluindo?', while keeping content clear, contextual and action-oriented without turning into diet prescription.
2.finalProject: This is a conceptual product case. The primary insight is that understanding increases when data, explanation and action live in the same decision block. Real-world validation with fitness users would be the next important step.
2.conclusion: Comportamento de treino → interpretação de métricas → tomada de decisão → retenção. The project demonstrates how a fitness product can transform complex metrics into clearer decisions and create a more understandable experience around progress. Feedback drives engagement. Personalization needs to be dynamic rather than static. Monetization should enhance the experience rather than create unnecessary friction. Clear feedback can connect user behavior, interpretation and motivation. The next step is to validate the experience with real users, refine AI-generated feedback and continue exploring how design systems influence behavior and sustain motivation.

3.title: DN Jeans
3.overview: DN Jeans is a product-discovery experience designed to help customers browse catalog items, compare options and move more easily toward purchase without unnecessary friction.
3.challenge: The challenge was to make product discovery clearer and less frustrating, helping users find the right product and decide faster without forcing a traditional e-commerce flow that did not match the brand's real behavior.
3.process: This project was originally a visual and product-design effort, not a complete formal UX research process. The structure below is a retrospective UX reconstruction used to clarify how the product journey could be strengthened without pretending the original project had completed formal research or wireframing.

designSprint.description: Mapped how customers searched, compared and selected items before purchase.
Defined the central opportunity: reduce friction between product discovery and purchase.
Structured the catalog around categories, filters, product details and a clear purchase escalation path.
Reviewed whether the product path could be clearer and whether shopping decisions could be supported earlier in the flow.
Refined the product journey so browsing, comparison and product information moved more smoothly toward decision-making.

3.myRole: UX strategy and visual product design

certainties: Customers need a clearer path from discovery to purchase
Product comparison becomes easier when filters and product information are visible together
The original brand behavior relied on direct contact and conversational conversion
suppositions: A cleaner product grid could reduce browsing friction
More explicit product information would support faster decision making
A WhatsApp-based conversion path would fit the actual sales behavior better than a full cart flow
doubts: This project did not originally include a complete formal UX research and wireframing process
A larger catalog could require a different purchase architecture in the future

3.userFlow: Discovery → Browse → Filter → Compare → Inspect product → Evaluate information → Decide → Purchase.

personas.name: Instagram customer
personas.pain: Has to repeat the same questions and determine product fit without a clear or centralized path to purchase.
personas.goal: Browse the collection, compare options and decide quickly with the information available.

userStories.story: As a browsing customer, I want to filter and compare products clearly so that I can decide faster without repeated clarification.

problemDefinitions.definition: Needs a clearer product-discovery flow because the lack of structured browsing and comparison creates friction before purchase.

craftNotes.conventions: The visual foundation stays consistent with a familiar e-commerce rhythm: product categories, imagery, pricing and decision-oriented product details.
craftNotes.affordances: Filters, product attributes and action CTAs stay visible and easy to evaluate to reduce hesitation mid-browse.
craftNotes.equity: The flow respects the brand's real conversion behavior by keeping the close-out step in WhatsApp rather than forcing a cart-based checkout model.
craftNotes.testing: No formal usability testing data exists for the original project, so this is framed as a proposed UX improvement rather than a claimed validated outcome.

3.solution: The proposed direction strengthens product discovery by making filtering, comparison and product information clearer, while aligning the purchase flow with the brand's actual WhatsApp-based conversion behavior. The goal is not to reinvent the business model, but to reduce friction between browsing and deciding.
3.finalProject: This project was originally a visual and product design effort, not a complete formal UX research and wireframing process. The design direction is therefore strongest as a UX clarification and strategic improvement rather than as a claim of completed validation. The next step would be real research, usability testing and a more formal information architecture review.
3.conclusion: Descoberta → filtros → comparação → informação do produto → decisão de compra. The project demonstrates how an e-commerce experience can reduce friction by improving product discovery and helping users move more clearly from browsing toward purchase. The core UX focus is product discovery, filtering, comparison, product information and decision-making. The visual foundation is strong, but the next important step would be strengthening the UX process through research, validation and usability testing.

4.title: ImovePro
4.overview: Multi-profile real estate marketplace (buyer/seller, agent, company) with radius-based geographic search and an interactive map, replacing traditional city/neighborhood filters.
4.challenge: Real estate agents manage leads, schedules, and communication across disconnected tools (WhatsApp, spreadsheets, separate calendars), while buyers rely on shallow location filters that don't reflect their real area of interest.
4.process: In-person discovery with all three marketplace profiles. We decided to treat each profile as a visually distinct workspace (not a single dashboard with permissions) to reduce cognitive load — each one sees only what it needs in its own context.

designSprint.description: Discovery with all three marketplace profiles, identifying fragmented lead management as a bigger pain point than search itself.
Decision to treat each profile as a visually distinct workspace instead of a single dashboard with permissions.
Designed the three dashboards, Kanban/table lead pipeline, and radius-based geolocated search.
Moderated in-person test with all three profiles, confirming they found core functions without prior guidance.
Delivered as a product proposal, with the dark/light design system tension documented as a next step.

4.myRole: UX/UI Designer responsible for designing the three dashboards, navigation architecture, lead pipeline, and geolocated search.

certainties: Agents treat fragmented lead management as the biggest pain point, not search itself
Buyers treat precise geographic discovery as decisive in choosing a platform
suppositions: Consolidating leads, schedule, and chat into one dashboard would reduce forgotten follow-ups
Radius search with an interactive map would increase perceived relevance of results
doubts: Would three visually distinct workspaces (different colors/themes per profile) hold up at scale without fragmenting the design system?

4.userFlow: Agent: lead enters the pipeline (New → Contacted → In Negotiation → Closed) → schedule and chat in the same dashboard → alert for follow-ups pending over 24h. Buyer: selects a workspace → searches by radius on the map → filters by type/budget → requests a quote.

personas.name: Real estate agent
personas.pain: Switches between WhatsApp, spreadsheet, and a separate calendar to know which leads have gone cold.
personas.goal: See the entire lead pipeline in a single dashboard, without cross-referencing multiple tools.

personas.name: Buyer/Seller
personas.role: End user looking for a property
personas.pain: Traditional neighborhood/city filters don't reflect their real area of interest.
personas.goal: Find options genuinely close to where they need to be, via radius map search.

userStories.story: As a real estate agent, I want to see my entire lead pipeline in one dashboard so that I don't lose follow-ups scattered across different tools.
As a buyer, I want to search for properties by real geographic radius so that I only see options that actually fit my routine.

problemDefinitions.definition: Is an independent professional who loses follow-ups across fragmented tools and needs a single pipeline because it reduces business risk and saves operational time.
Is an end user frustrated by shallow location filters who needs precise geographic search because it increases the perceived relevance of results and speeds up the decision.

craftNotes.conventions: The lead pipeline follows the Kanban pattern already familiar to any management-tool user (Trello, Notion), reducing the training needed for agents.
craftNotes.affordances: Map pins change color/size based on property type, and the search radius is directly draggable on the map, making filter manipulation tactile and immediate instead of relying on numeric fields.
craftNotes.equity: Each profile (agent, buyer, company) sees only the information relevant to its context, reducing cognitive load especially for users less familiar with dense dashboards.
craftNotes.testing: Moderated in-person test with all three profiles simultaneously, checking whether each one found its core function without accidentally crossing into another profile's information.

4.solution: Three distinct dashboards (Agent, Buyer/Seller, Company) with shared visual identity. Lead pipeline in Kanban and table views, pending follow-up alerts, radius search with an interactive map and custom pins.
4.finalProject: NO QUANTIFIED METRIC — no formal agile process documented (unlike TI Help), no numeric success rate, no production conversion data. A moderated in-person test qualitatively confirmed participants across all three profiles found the system's core functions without prior guidance. Unresolved design system tension: dark background (Agent/Company) and light background (Buyer) share an accent color but not full tokens.

5.title: Yacht Booking
5.overview: Conceptual app for booking yachts and premium maritime experiences, exploring high-end design for a luxury audience.
5.challenge: Create a digital experience that conveys exclusivity, security, and sophistication for very high-value transactions — where trust is everything.
5.process: Luxury market research, benchmark analysis of premium apps (Porsche, Net-A-Porter, Soho House), defining a visual and interaction language that communicated exclusivity without excess.

designSprint.description: Luxury market research and benchmarking of premium apps (Porsche, Net-A-Porter, Soho House) to map an exclusivity visual language.
Defined the design principle 'exclusivity without excess,' prioritizing editorial curation over traditional listings.
Prototyped 40 screens with an immersive gallery, discreet identity verification, and a simplified 4-tap booking flow.
Internal validation of visual language and flow against reference benchmarks, without real user testing (self-directed project).
Full design system documentation and case presentation as a portfolio exercise.

5.myRole: Self-directed design exploration project. Responsible for the full conceptualization, research, visual language definition, prototyping, and design system documentation.

certainties: Luxury audiences have very high expectations for visual and interaction quality
Security and identity verification are non-negotiable for this audience
Information overload and visual clutter communicate a lack of sophistication
suppositions: A minimalist interface communicates better quality than a dense one
Premium gestures and micro-interactions would differentiate from competitors
Editorial curation would be more effective than a traditional listing
doubts: How far to push simplification without losing information essential to the decision?
What's the right level of personalization to avoid feeling intrusive?
Would dark mode be perceived as more premium than light mode for this audience?

5.userFlow: User accesses an editorial of experiences → selects destination/period → views the yacht via an immersive gallery → checks real-time availability → identity verification → secure payment → confirmation with a dedicated concierge.

personas.name: Eduardo Ximenes
personas.pain: Generic platforms don't convey the trust and exclusivity he expects for this spending category.
personas.goal: Book a unique maritime experience with the ease of an Uber but the standard of a 5-star hotel.

personas.name: Catarina Mello
personas.pain: Managing bookings, maintenance, and availability of multiple yachts across different, disconnected systems.
personas.goal: A centralized platform to manage the entire operation with real-time visibility.

userStories.story: As a high-net-worth businessman, I want to book a maritime experience with few taps and high trust so that I feel the service matches the value I'm paying.
As a fleet manager, I want centralized visibility of bookings and maintenance so that I don't carry operational risk from scattered information.

problemDefinitions.definition: Is a high-net-worth businessman who needs a minimalist, secure booking experience because perceived exclusivity is decisive in this spending category.
Is a fleet manager dealing with disconnected systems who needs a centralized platform because it reduces operational risk and provides real-time visibility.

craftNotes.conventions: Followed already-validated luxury app conventions (serif typography for titles, generous spacing, restrained palette) to communicate sophistication without reinventing visual patterns.
craftNotes.affordances: Booking elements use subtle micro-interactions (fade, slight scale) instead of abrupt feedback, communicating 'premium' through the interface's own behavior, not just static aesthetics.
craftNotes.equity: Even in a luxury niche product, identity verification was designed to feel smooth and non-intimidating, avoiding unnecessary friction for users less accustomed to digital KYC processes.
craftNotes.testing: As a self-directed project with no real client, validation was done through structured comparison against market benchmarks (Porsche, Net-A-Porter, Soho House) instead of traditional usability testing — a limitation I state openly in interviews.

5.solution: Editorial interface curating experiences instead of a product list. Immersive video gallery for each yacht. Simplified 4-tap booking process. Smooth, discreet identity verification. Digital concierge available 24/7 via chat.
5.finalProject: Complete conceptual project with a documented design system, 40 prototyped screens, and a case presentation. Deep exploration of premium micro-interactions and high-end visual language as a portfolio exercise.

6.title: Solar Panel Monitoring
6.overview: Conceptual landing page for solar energy businesses, built as a design product — not from research with real solar energy clients, but as an exercise in translating complex technical data into an accessible value proposition, with a payback calculator and lead generation via WhatsApp/Instagram.
6.challenge: A solar energy business needs to convert visitors into qualified WhatsApp/Instagram contacts, but the market communicates in technical metrics (kWh, generation peak, efficiency) that don't mean much to the average homeowner — who just wants to understand if they'll save money, how long the investment takes to pay off, and whether the service is worth hiring.
6.process: Reference research across existing energy and sustainability sites/apps on the market (benchmark, not original field research), defining a value proposition and information hierarchy that prioritized human language ('You could save X per month') over raw technical units (kWh), including a payback calculator built directly into the page, with direct WhatsApp and Instagram CTAs at strategic points.

designSprint.description: Benchmarked existing energy/sustainability sites and apps, mapping how the market communicates technical data today.
Defined a value proposition centered on savings language (currency/month) instead of raw technical units (kWh).
Prototyped the landing page with an embedded payback calculator and direct WhatsApp/Instagram CTAs.
Internal validation of information hierarchy against the benchmarks gathered, without testing with a real solar energy client.
Finalized as a design product template for sale on Gumroad/UI8/Figma Community.

6.myRole: Self-directed project, built as a template for sale (Gumroad/UI8/Figma Community). Responsible for the full conceptualization, data visualization system, and end-to-end flow prototyping.

certainties: Technical terms like 'kWh' and 'generation peak' aren't understood by the average homeowner
Comparisons with the previous period are more readable than isolated absolute values
Investment payback time is the central question blocking the homeowner's purchase decision
suppositions: Translating technical data into savings language (currency/month) would increase comprehension and engagement with the page
An interactive payback calculator on the page would increase trust and contact conversion rate compared to just stating estimated savings in text
doubts: Without a real solar energy client validating the product, would the proposed information hierarchy hold up in a real usability test?
Would the calculator's accuracy (based on which inputs — average consumption, region, system size?) hold up against a simulation done by a real installer?

6.userFlow: Visitor lands on the page → understands the savings benefit in plain language (not raw kWh) → uses the payback calculator to simulate how long the investment takes to pay off → views the products/services offered by the business → is directed to contact via WhatsApp or Instagram with one tap.

personas.name: Homeowner interested in solar energy
personas.role: Landing page visitor, potential business customer
personas.pain: Doesn't understand solar energy's technical data and doesn't know if the investment is really worth it or how long it takes to pay off.
personas.goal: Simulate how much they'll save and how long it takes to recoup the investment, simply, and easily contact the seller/installer.

userStories.story: As a homeowner, I want to simulate my savings in plain language so that I can decide to hire the service without needing to understand kWh.

problemDefinitions.definition: Is a visitor unfamiliar with solar energy who needs a payback calculator in accessible language because it reduces the uncertainty blocking their purchase decision.

craftNotes.conventions: The calculator follows the already-familiar pattern of financial simulators (numeric input + real-time highlighted result), reducing the learning curve for anyone who's used a loan or financing simulator.
craftNotes.affordances: The average-consumption slider gives immediate visual feedback (the savings value updates in real time as the user drags), reinforcing cause-and-effect without needing instruction.
craftNotes.equity: Page language deliberately avoids technical jargon to not exclude the average homeowner, who is the real purchase-decision audience — not the technical installer.
craftNotes.testing: Without a real client validating it, testing was limited to reviewing information hierarchy and language clarity against benchmarks — a limitation I state openly: it lacks validation with a real solar energy user.

6.solution: Landing page with accessible language instead of raw technical units, a payback calculator showing how long the investment takes to pay off, a clear presentation of the business's products and services, and direct WhatsApp/Instagram CTAs — designed to generate qualified leads for a solar energy business.
6.finalProject: Design product template, built for sale (not implemented with a real solar energy client). No real usage metric — it's an exercise in information hierarchy, a payback calculator, and lead generation, not a case with a validated business outcome.

7.title: Social Media Design & Content Strategy
7.overview: This was a real-world social media design and content strategy project focused on understanding which content types generate attention and engagement and how they should be distributed across formats.
7.challenge: The challenge was to create content that was visually effective while also understanding the relationship between topic, format, day, time, caption, distribution and audience response.
7.process: Context → Diagnosis → Strategy → Visual System → Content → Validation → Iteration. The work combined analysis of existing content performance with the strategic packaging of ideas across feed, stories and reels.

designSprint.description: Reviewed the current content base and observed which formats and topics were already gaining attention.
Mapped performance patterns by day, time, format and caption to identify the strongest strategic levers.
Built a more consistent content system based on audience response, repetition and reuse of material across channels.
Defined a visual language that could support different content pieces without losing recognition.
Organized topic, format and distribution into a repeatable production model.
Checked which assets performed best and how they could be reused in stories or feed content.
Adjusted the strategy based on real response patterns and improved reuse opportunities.

7.myRole: Design and content strategy for a real-world social media operation

certainties: Performance varies according to day and time
Format, caption and topic influence performance
Municipal problems that are not always highly perceived can generate interest when communicated clearly
suppositions: Reels and feed posts can be reused strategically in Stories
A stronger visual system would create more consistency across content pieces
The same message can be adapted into multiple formats without losing its core meaning
doubts: The strongest performance drivers are context-specific and should be revisited over time
Not all recurring topics perform equally across all audiences and publication windows

7.userFlow: Topic → Content format → Publication → Audience response → Reuse / redistribution.

personas.name: Local audience
personas.pain: Receives too many repetitive posts and responds more strongly to content that is clear, timely and relevant.
personas.goal: Encounter information that feels useful, visually clear and relevant to the moment.

userStories.story: As a local audience member, I want content that is relevant to my context and easy to understand so that I can engage with it and share it when it matters.

problemDefinitions.definition: Needs a more strategic and consistent communication system because the relationship between topic, timing and format directly affects whether content gets attention and engagement.

craftNotes.conventions: The content system relies on patterns already recognizable in social platforms: short-form visual hierarchy, clear hooks, reuse across placements and strong caption structure.
craftNotes.affordances: Posts were designed to be adaptable across feed, reel and story surfaces without losing the message or recognition.
craftNotes.equity: The strategy focused on communication clarity over vanity metrics, turning content into a repeatable system and not just a series of isolated posts.
craftNotes.testing: The stated performance data for this case is +29% and 10K views, as documented in the project record. No additional metrics were added.

7.solution: The project transformed performance observations into a more consistent content strategy and visual communication system. It organized the content operation around topic, format, timing, caption, distribution and audience response, allowing posts to be reused strategically across multiple placements. The design effort was not limited to aesthetics; it supported a disciplined communication system.
7.finalProject: This was real-world work rather than a fictional UX exercise. The documented performance is +29% and 10K views. The project demonstrates the shift from simply producing posts to designing a repeatable content strategy based on observation, experimentation and iteration.
7.conclusion: Experiência real + dados + estratégia. The project demonstrates that social media design is not only about visual quality. Effective communication depends on understanding the relationship between topic, format, timing, caption, distribution and audience response. The strongest strategic insight came from connecting content performance with the way content is packaged and distributed. The cycle was: Problema → Observação → Hipótese → Experimento → Resultado → Aprendizado → Iteração. The project moved from producing isolated posts to designing a repeatable content strategy grounded in performance and iteration.
